cultivar: Yunnan large-leaf populations of the Wuliang range, with semi-wild and wild-type trees in the higher forest
processing: Raw pu-erh: pan-fired, rolled, sun-dried maocha pressed into cakes or tuo; the Nanjian factories at the northern end of the range press much of it into tuo.
harvest_season: Spring (late March to April) for the best lots; the mountain's cool altitude makes the first flush later than in Xishuangbanna.
appearance_dry: Slim, dark, lightly twisted leaves with silver buds and a few long stems, pressed into a medium cake.
appearance_wet: Smallish, soft, yellow-green leaves with a slightly uneven look from mixed-age trees.
taste_profile: Light and elegant: fresh flowers and honey, a mild clean bitterness, little astringency, a medium-light body and a cool, lingering sweetness that reads as 'wild'.

brewing.notes: Rinse once. Porcelain, short steeps and a light hand; this is a tea of aroma and finish, and heavy leafing just makes it taste thin and green.

vintage_note: Sold by spring harvest year and county or township (Jingdong townships such as Anding and Manwan, Nanjian, Zhenyuan's Wuliang side), as cakes from small producers and as tuo from the Nanjian factories, which carry production years like any factory product. It is drunk young (1–5 years) and gets honeyed in the 5–12-year window; genuinely old Wuliang mostly means 1990s–2000s Nanjian tuo, since named Wuliang cakes only became common after about 2005. Supply is 2005–2025 and dry-stored, and because old trees here are plentiful and cheap it is one of the honest bargains of the gushu market.
description:
The Wuliang mountains run from Nanjian in Dali prefecture down through Jingdong, Zhenyuan and Jinggu in Pu'er prefecture, and they are the big, cool, forested range on the west of the Ailao valley. Tea here grows high, often above 1,800 m, among forest, and the result is a light, elegant sheng that people describe as wild even when it comes from planted gardens.

The leaf is on the small side for Yunnan and comes from mixed-age trees, a lot of them genuinely old because the mountain was never fully turned into plantations. Processing is standard sheng, pan-fired, rolled and sun-dried, and the northern end of the range has a long tuo tradition through the Nanjian factories, whose Tulin Phoenix tuo are a Wuliang tea in nest form.

In the cup Wuliang is fresh flowers and honey with a mild bitterness, barely any astringency and a cool sweetness that hangs around; the body is lighter than Menghai or Mengku tea, so it is judged on finesse. It is forgiving and brews well with short steeps, and it is the kind of sheng that makes sense of the phrase 'high mountain' when you taste it next to a flatland plantation tea.

Sold by spring year and township, mostly at modest prices, and 'Wuliang Shan gushu' is one of the cheapest genuine old-tree labels in Yunnan, precisely because the area is less famous. The things to watch are thinness (the lower gardens make pleasant but watery tea) and wrappers that upgrade it to Jingmai or Yiwu. The Nanjian tuo are a cheap way to taste the mountain with some age on it.

For contrast, drink it next to an Ailao Shan tea from the other side of the valley: close cousins, with Ailao a little wilder and cooler.
